title: I’m making an isometric soulslike that runs in the browser on my own WebGPU engine
author: dpsmkr7
selftext:
**Chasm** is an isometric soulslike set in a dark fantasy world.

You start as a knight with a rusty sword at the mouth of a cave and fight your way down through the whole dungeon to the goblin chieftain’s throne room. Along the way you level up, loot chests and take better weapons from the fallen.

Once the dungeon is cleared, the open world begins.

The game runs on my own WebGPU engine: volumetric lighting, real-time cloth physics for capes and banners, ragdolls, and shader-based water and lava. It plays right in the browser, including on phones.

It’s still in development: one dungeon and the start of the open world are done.

Play: [https://chasm.layero.app/](https://chasm.layero.app/) 

(0.5 GB, All modern browsers except Firefox)

comments.author: FailedGradAdmissions
comments.body:
Ngl don’t let indie games see this or they’ll go nuclear. Yeah, that’s a good thing. Best webgpu ai game I’ve seen in a while. But note that utilizing webGPU makes it harder for your game to go into mobile and consoles. For a portfolio game that you want to only share with friends and that’s non issue, but if you ever do want to release on mobile it’ll be an uphill battle to optimize.

Other than that, play your own game if you haven’t already and tweak the balance and mechanics. In actual game dev a big part of the development process is balancing and making it fun. That’s the “feel” of the game, and not something you can necessarily offload to agents yet. I mean you could, but while Claude passing the level could help you make sure a level is bug free, there’s no way it would know if it was “fun”.
